Its sound sits between the plainness of a shepherd's pipe and the refinement of a professional woodwind, and it can carry both lively, cheerful melodies and deep, finely shaded feeling. Sopilka is the name Ukrainian folk players give to an aerophone of the end-blown flute family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.111-12. The commonest is a small pipe with six to ten finger holes, traditionally made of elder or guelder rose wood; the word also covers related folk instruments that have a fipple mouthpiece and a narrowed end, close to the recorder. It is common in folk ensembles recreating the traditional music of the various ethnic groups of western Ukraine, especially the Hutsuls of the Carpathian Mountains; players often play several together, and they can also imitate natural sounds such as birdsong and insects.
索皮爾卡笛為烏克蘭氣鳴樂器。已知最早實物以猛獁象牙製成，屬舊石器時代；11世紀故: The sopilka is a Ukrainian aerophone. The earliest known example is made of mammoth ivory and belongs to the Palaeolithic period; stories and paintings of the eleventh century already depict it, such as the murals of Saint Sophia's Cathedral in Kyiv. Early on it was mainly a folk instrument, played by shepherds, in trio groupings or at weddings, and it is mentioned in Lesya Ukrainka's play The Forest Song. It is also used in folk ensembles of western Ukraine, especially among the Hutsuls of the Carpathian Mountains. After a ten-hole fingering instrument was developed in 1967 it entered the Ukrainian music education system and was taken up in pop performances by folk rock groups such as Kobza; since then it has also appeared with folk electronica acts and pop singers.
索皮爾卡笛為烏克蘭端吹笛類氣鳴樂器，Hornbostel–Sachs 編號 42: The sopilka is a Ukrainian end-blown aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.111-12. Its common form is a small pipe, the traditional body usually made of elder or guelder rose wood; there are also early examples made of mammoth bone. Related folk instruments close to the recorder have a fipple mouthpiece and a narrowed end, but the source does not record what the mouthpiece, the edges of the finger holes or the other parts are made of; nor does it describe the body material of the modern ten-hole instrument.
